scenes.tts: Sleep pressure is highest when you fall asleep, and it drains all night. What does a recording show?
scenes.visual: The two-process sawtooth from chapter one, zoomed to one night: the pressure curve falls. On-screen question: what does a recording show?
scenes.narration: Sleep pressure is highest when you fall asleep, and it drains all night. What does a recording show?

scenes.tts: Sleep is read from brain waves, eye movements and chin muscle tone. The night is cut into thirty-second windows.
scenes.caption: Sleep is read from brain waves, eye movements and chin muscle tone. The night is cut into 30-second windows.
scenes.visual: Three stacked traces labelled EEG, EOG, EMG. A 30-second window slides along them, and each window gets one stage label.
scenes.narration: Sleep is read from brain waves, eye movements and chin muscle tone. The night is cut into 30-second windows.

scenes.tts: Slower, larger brain waves mean many cortical neurons are active, then silent, in step. That happens as non-rem sleep deepens.
scenes.visual: Three schematic panels. Waking panel: example beta trace and eyes-closed alpha trace, labelled waking. NREM panel: example N1 theta, N2 spindles and K-complexes, N3 slow waves, slowing and growing left to right, labelled NREM deepening. A separate REM panel off to one side, not on the depth scale. All traces labelled schematic.
scenes.narration: Slower, larger brain waves mean many cortical neurons are active, then silent, in step. That happens as NREM sleep deepens.
scenes.caption: Slower, larger brain waves mean many cortical neurons are active, then silent, in step. That happens as NREM sleep deepens.

scenes.tts: In stage N three, the deepest, large slow waves take up at least a fifth of the window.
scenes.caption: In stage N3, the deepest, large slow waves take up at least a fifth of the window.
scenes.visual: An N3 epoch: big slow waves. On screen: 0.5 to 2 Hz, peak-to-peak above 75 microvolts in frontal leads, at least 20% of the epoch.
scenes.narration: In stage N3, the deepest, large slow waves take up at least a fifth of the window.

scenes.tts: In rem sleep, the brain waves can look much like waking. The eyes and the muscles tell them apart.
scenes.caption: In REM sleep, the brain waves can look much like waking. The eyes and the muscles tell them apart.
scenes.visual: Side by side, a waking epoch and a REM epoch: similar EEG; the REM epoch shows rapid eye movements and a flat, low muscle trace.
scenes.narration: In REM sleep, the brain waves can look much like waking. The eyes and the muscles tell them apart.

scenes.tts: So where in the night will most of the deepest sleep fall?
scenes.visual: An empty hypnogram for one night, split into first half and second half. On-screen question: where does N3 fall?
scenes.narration: So where in the night will most of the deepest sleep fall?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Early, when pressure is highest. Rem sleep grows toward morning, with the clock and with time already asleep.
scenes.caption: Early, when pressure is highest. REM sleep grows toward morning, with the clock and with time already asleep.
scenes.visual: The hypnogram builds: N3 blocks bunch in the first half; REM bars lengthen toward morning. The draining pressure curve is drawn underneath.
scenes.narration: Early, when pressure is highest. REM sleep grows toward morning, with the clock and with time already asleep.

scenes.tts: How does the brain flip? In one model, sleep-active neurons and wake-promoting groups inhibit each other.
scenes.visual: A seesaw: a sleep side labelled VLPO and a wake side labelled wake-promoting groups, with inhibitory arrows each way.
scenes.narration: How does the brain flip? In one model, sleep-active neurons and wake-promoting groups inhibit each other.

scenes.tts: Whichever side is ahead silences the other. So the brain flips quickly, instead of drifting.
scenes.visual: The seesaw snaps from one side to the other with no pause in the middle.
scenes.narration: Whichever side is ahead silences the other. So the brain flips quickly, instead of drifting.

scenes.tts: Once sleep wins, pressure must drain well below where sleep began before waking can win again. That memory is one way to picture the gap between the two levels.
scenes.visual: The seesaw beside the two-process graph; the gap between the upper and lower lines is highlighted.
scenes.narration: Once sleep wins, pressure must drain well below where sleep began before waking can win again. That memory is one way to picture the gap between the two levels.

scenes.tts: Orexin neurons are thought to hold the switch on the wake side, like a finger holding a light switch up.
scenes.visual: A finger labelled orexin holds a wall switch in the up position, labelled wake.
scenes.narration: Orexin neurons are thought to hold the switch on the wake side, like a finger holding a light switch up.

scenes.tts: In narcolepsy type one, these neurons are severely reduced, and waking becomes unstable. Muscle tone can also fail while the person stays conscious.
scenes.caption: In narcolepsy type 1, these neurons are severely reduced, and waking becomes unstable. Muscle tone can also fail while the person stays conscious.
scenes.visual: The finger lifts away; the switch flickers and a wake bar breaks into short bouts. A figure slumps with eyes open. Label: cataplexy, consciousness preserved.
scenes.narration: In narcolepsy type 1, these neurons are severely reduced, and waking becomes unstable. Muscle tone can also fail while the person stays conscious.

scenes.tts: Keep this. Deep sleep mainly follows the pressure. Rem grows with the clock and with time asleep. A switch with a memory may explain the gap that keeps sleep in one block.
scenes.caption: Keep this. Deep sleep mainly follows the pressure. REM grows with the clock and with time asleep. A switch with a memory may explain the gap that keeps sleep in one block.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the hypnogram, the pressure curve and the seesaw together.
scenes.narration: Keep this. Deep sleep mainly follows the pressure. REM grows with the clock and with time asleep. A switch with a memory may explain the gap that keeps sleep in one block.
